findings.description: vfs.write() is not awaited. If the VFS write method is asynchronous (returns a Promise), the function returns a checkpoint before the write is confirmed to have succeeded. Any rejection from vfs.write() becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than propagating to the caller, and the checkpoint string would falsely indicate a successful write. This can cause data loss (silent write failures) and leave the system in an inconsistent state where the checkpoint references content that was never persisted.

No path validation or sanitization is performed on input.path before passing to the VFS. While the VFS overlay may provide containment, defense-in-depth principles suggest the tool should at minimum reject paths containing null bytes or validate against expected path formats. If the VFS implementation does not strictly canonicalize and confine paths, this could enable path traversal (e.g., '../' sequences or absolute paths escaping the overlay root).

No input validation: if input.content is undefined/null, Buffer.from() will throw a TypeError with an unhelpful message; if input.path is undefined, behavior depends entirely on the VFS. A malformed-input guard would produce clearer errors and avoid leaking internal stack traces to callers.

independent_verifier.summary: The implementation is minimal and delegates most responsibility to the VFS. The primary concern is the missing await on vfs.write(), which—if the VFS write is asynchronous—means the checkpoint is returned before persistence is confirmed and write errors are silently swallowed as unhandled rejections. Path validation is also absent, relying entirely on the VFS for traversal protection. Recommend awaiting the write call and adding basic input/path validation.
